target: Deep dive: Mortgage lender underwriting help-desk / scenario-desk log, US agency lending (ranked third). Refutation conducted with WebSearch exhausted and all regulator, GSE, vendor and press hosts blocked; every sourced check below is against a GitHub- or npm-hosted artefact fetched in this session (HMDA LAR spec, hmda-frontend README, esa-qa-mirror clone recomputed, LoanScope READMEs, three npm package manifests, mortctl); everything else is labelled recall or estimate and is not measurement.

refuted.point: The EBA Single Rulebook Q&A corpus 'brackets' the recurrence rate of lender scenario-desk questions ('about eight mortgage-related Q&As per year' used as a sourced analogue for how often settlements recur at the owner level).
refuted.why: The numbers reproduce exactly from a fresh clone (https://github.com/gnosifex/esa-qa-mirror, regulator corpus via third-party mirror, 2,166 files; 103 mention 'mortgage'; 43 under topic Credit risk; 5 cite GL/2020/06; median 317 days, min 31, max 2,585), but what they measure is unrelated to a lender's desk. Of the 103 mortgage Q&As only 6 contain any underwriting term (creditworthiness, loan origination, LTV, DSTI) and only one (2021_6130) concerns the loan-origination guidelines at all; the credit-risk items are CRR Articles 124, 125, 501, 178, 123, 208, i.e. capital treatment. The corpus is also thinning, not compounding: mortgage Q&As published per year were 3 in 2024, 3 in 2025 and 2 in 2026 to date (computed from the clone). A regulator's prudential-rule clarification rate says nothing about how often loan officers at one lender re-ask the same income or asset question. The analogue should be dropped from the recurrence section; it supports only the narrower H3/H8 point that owner-level loops are small and slow.

refuted.point: Encompass 'exposes conditions and rules through an API that third parties and lenders themselves build on', used both to say a ledger could export settlements 'to Encompass business rules and the PPE' and to say the system-of-record penalty is not triggered.
refuted.why: The fetched artefacts do not support a rules-export path. @this-npm-test-org/connection-encompass (npm manifest, created 2026-04-28, org literally named 'this-npm-test-org', README self-describes as 'Connects your agent to Encompass') lists loans, milestones, conditions, documents, rate locks and a 40 requests/second limit; @vqnguyen1/piece-icemortgage-encompass (npm, Activepieces piece) lists create/retrieve/update/delete loan, templates and field locks; @royal-united-mortgage/rum-sdk (npm, published 2026-09-14, repo README 404) exports encompass, optimalblue, paylocity, panterra, captivated, insellerate, settlementone, realeo clients generated from OpenAPI contracts. None mentions Encompass business rules, product guidelines or eligibility rules. The claim that a settlement could be pushed into LOS business rules by API is unsupported by anything fetched and rests on recall; the minimal product's step 3 therefore ends at a document, which is the incumbent overlay matrix.

refuted.point: 'Open-source rule encoders exist as independent projects (LoanScope, mortctl; fetched)' as evidence that the guide-to-rule encoding problem attracts builders.
refuted.why: mortctl (https://registry.npmjs.org/mortctl, npm, created 2026-02-26) is a command-line calculator for LTV, CLTV, PITI, county loan limits and PMI estimate with a five-programme eligibility check; it encodes no overlays, no income rules and no lender layer. Only LoanScope (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ramiisaac/loanscope/main/README.md, independent open-source project) models a lender override layer, and its repository metadata (stars, contributors, production use) could not be read (api.github.com returned 403 in this session), so it is one developer's modelling choice, not evidence about lender practice. The plural 'encoders' is one project.

weakened.point: 'FHA Refer files require manual underwriting by a DE underwriter by rule' listed as a severe H4 penalty and one of the three reasons the workflow ranks third.
weakened.why: The fact matches recall [RECALL, unverified; HUD 4000.1 blocked], but it does not distinguish this workflow: every agency file, including DU Approve/Eligible files, is signed off by a human underwriter who remains responsible for the file regardless of the AUS finding [RECALL, unverified]. The product never proposed to remove the underwriter, so the FHA Refer point is redundant with the general condition and should not carry separate weight. The general condition is the stronger negative: human review per file is 100 percent by structure, so a ledger can only shorten one question-and-answer exchange, never remove a decision.

weakened.point: 'The lender layer is bright-line overlay policy that rules engines already encode (LoanScope demonstrates the shape in open source)' as severe H3/H6 evidence.
weakened.why: The README quotes check out verbatim ('get hand-coded into spreadsheets and one-off scripts'; 18 first-class eligibility checks; mergeRules override-wins), but LoanScope's own scope statement says 'Declarative rules only ... No runtime rule DSL, no spreadsheet imports' and 'Underwriting rules never live in the database', so its lender layer is TypeScript that a credit-policy owner cannot edit; it is a developer's scenario and goal-seek CLI ('what if I pay down $X'), not a governance artefact. It shows that a developer chose to model overlays as numeric thresholds, which is consistent with recall of product matrices, but it is not evidence that lenders encode overlays adequately. The H3 conclusion should rest on recall of LOS business rules and PPE eligibility rules, flagged as such, not on this project.

weakened.point: Category H at 3 to 10 percent of desk questions, 'only over the lender's own overlays and internal policy', as the addressable share.
weakened.why: That share still overstates what a ledger adds. A question about an overlay that is already in the product matrix or PPE is a lookup (brief category 1, deterministic from existing rules), not H. H survives only where the matrix is silent, and the natural resolution of that case is a matrix or product-guideline edit, which is the instrument the credit-policy committee already uses at policy cadence. The ledger's increment over the matrix is the subset of H where the owner declines to edit the matrix but is willing to sign a standing answer, which is the IPSA pattern (repetition where bright lines already exist, discretion where disputes arise) restated. No number exists for that subset; the 3 to 10 percent is an upper bound on it, not an estimate of it.

weakened.point: The HMDA denial-reason enumeration (fields 68 to 71) as 'a weak external anchor' for the A share and for 'there is no code for guideline ambiguity'.
weakened.why: Fields 68 to 72 verified against https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cfpb/hmda-platform/master/docs/spec/Public_File_LAR_Spec.csv (government open-source documentation): DTI, employment history, credit history, collateral, insufficient cash, unverifiable information, application incomplete, MI denied, other, not applicable. These are Regulation C adverse-outcome categories reported per denied application for fair-lending purposes; they classify why a borrower was denied, not why a desk was asked anything, and would not show interpretation or missing documents on approved files either. The anchor carries no information about desk composition and should be removed; the A share is a pure estimate. Note also that the deep dive lowered A from the finder's 40 to 50 percent to 30 to 40 percent without any new evidence.

weakened.point: 'The workflow keeps its third-place ranking only because it is the one lending workflow whose historical log could be sampled cheaply'; 'a single lender's twelve-month desk log would settle the question in two weeks'.
weakened.why: The access premise is unproven and structurally doubtful. Scenario emails and Teams threads carry borrower nonpublic personal information (names, income, account balances) that lenders must protect under GLBA and Regulation P [RECALL, unverified], so a de-identified export is a legal and engineering task before sampling begins; the cluster finder's own row records desk volumes as 'not public ... would need customer discovery'. Classification also needs a senior underwriter to distinguish a lookup from an interpretive question, i.e. the scarce resource the product targets. 'Cheap' is asserted, not shown, and it is the sole stated reason for the ranking.

weakened.point: 'Guide changes arrive roughly monthly, which resets some settlements', offered as a positive for the ledger's diff-and-re-ratify feature.
weakened.why: Cadence is recall [RECALL, unverified; selling-guide.fanniemae.com and guide.freddiemac.com blocked], and each announcement touches specific sections; the income, asset and rental-income sections that generate the recurring hard cases change rarely, so most settlements would not be reset [RECALL, unverified]. Where they do change, the owner ships the change with a redlined guide and effective date [RECALL, unverified], and guideline-search vendors already sell change alerts [RECALL, vendors blocked]. The diff feature is a commodity, not a reason to build.

weakened.point: 'Third-party connector packages describing a vendor API' rated as weak but sourced evidence for the Encompass API surface.
weakened.why: Weaker than stated: the principal package sits in an npm organisation named 'this-npm-test-org' and was created five months ago; the '40 requests per second (Encompass standard)' figure is that package's own README assertion with no ICE documentation behind it. The Royal United Mortgage SDK confirms that one lender does vendor-integration engineering (exports for Encompass, Optimal Blue, Paylocity and five others; README says clients are regenerated from OpenAPI contracts in the repo), which says nothing about a desk or about rules. Treat both as existence proofs of an API, not as specification.

strengthened.point: The ROI arithmetic and its negative conclusion.
strengthened.why: Recomputed: 10,000 loans x 0.5 questions x 0.25 hours x 75 dollars = 93,750 dollars; H at 3 to 7 percent = 2,813 to 6,563 dollars; 20 percent = 18,750 dollars; a lender ten times larger = 28,000 to 66,000 dollars, 187,500 at 20 percent (analyst arithmetic, all inputs estimates). The stronger observation the deep dive does not draw out: 1,250 hours is about 0.6 FTE. At a 10,000-loan lender the entire desk, at 100 percent capture, is under one senior underwriter, so no plausible H share supports standalone pricing, and even quadrupling the question rate to 2 per loan leaves H at 7 percent worth roughly 26,000 dollars (estimate). The economics fail before the H debate starts.

strengthened.point: The EBA corpus numbers as evidence for H3/H8 at the owner level.
strengthened.why: Every figure in the key-numbers entry reproduced exactly from a fresh clone (2,166; CRR 2,003, CRD 96, DORA 67; 103; 43; 5; median 317, min 31, max 2,585; https://github.com/gnosifex/esa-qa-mirror, regulator corpus via third-party mirror with eba.europa.eu source URLs per record). Corpus-wide median submission-to-final is 248 days (n=2,147, computed). The correct use of this evidence is narrow and it holds: the one owner-run, prospective, versioned interpretation loop that can be measured in lending regulation is small, slow and free to the regulated firm.

strengthened.point: HMDA LAR spec citations (AUS names fields 96 to 101; AUS result codes fields 102 to 107; hmda-frontend 'millions of HMDA records per year').
strengthened.why: All verified verbatim against https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cfpb/hmda-platform/master/docs/spec/Public_File_LAR_Spec.csv and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cfpb/hmda-frontend/master/README.md (government open-source documentation). AUS codes are DU, LP, TOTAL Scorecard, GUS, Other, Not applicable; result codes include Approve/Eligible, Approve/Ineligible, Refer/Eligible, Refer/Ineligible, Refer with Caution, Out of Scope, Error, Accept, Caution, Ineligible, Incomplete, Invalid, Refer, Eligible, Unable to Determine, Other, Not applicable. The structural point stands: federal reporting is built around owner-run automated underwriting systems as the executable guide.

strengthened.point: 'The largest interpretive bucket is agency-guide meaning that the lender cannot settle authoritatively and that the owner is encoding itself.'
strengthened.why: LoanScope's README lists 'departure-residence rental income' and 'self-employed 24-month averaging' among the edge cases it encodes deterministically (fetched), which shows that the areas the deep dive calls interpretive are treated by at least one builder as guide-determined calculations. The owner side goes further than the deep dive states: Fannie Mae Form 1084 and Freddie Mac Form 91 are owner-published cash-flow worksheets for self-employment income, Ask Poli is an owner-run searchable Q&A layer, and the Income Calculator and AIM add rep-and-warrant relief [all RECALL, unverified; fanniemae.com and freddiemac.com blocked]. Bucket C is served free by the owner, before any lender ledger exists.

strengthened.point: The verifier's kill threshold ('a clear majority of repeat questions must concern the lender's own policy') is judged unlikely to be met.
strengthened.why: The deep dive's own A to H split has lender-policy H at 3 to 10 percent against guide-meaning C at 20 to 30 percent and missing-evidence A at 30 to 40 percent (estimates). For the threshold to be met, the structural ratio between C and H would have to invert, which nothing found or recalled supports. The prior against the workflow is the deep dive's own numbers, and the only measurement that could overturn it is one the deep dive shows is not cheap to get.

missing: DU and LPA findings reports already tell the processor which documents each file needs [RECALL, unverified]; the A bucket (30 to 40 percent, estimate) is therefore largely answered by the owner's AUS before any desk question, so the desk's A traffic is duplication of an existing artefact, not an unmet need. The deep dive treats A only as a penalty, not as already-served demand.

Correspondent and aggregator overlays: a mid-size IMB selling loans to aggregators or non-delegated investors is bound by those buyers' overlays and guides as well as the GSEs' [RECALL, unverified], adding further owners who are not the buyer of the product. The deep dive mentions investor guidelines in passing but does not count them in the ownership objection.

Non-agency lending (non-QM, portfolio, jumbo) is the only mortgage segment where the lender owns the guide and the ownership objection disappears; the deep dive scopes it out without saying that the third-place ranking is therefore scope-induced. Non-agency is a small share of US originations [RECALL, unverified], so it likely fails on volume instead, but that should be stated.

No EU or French volume, desk structure or cost was examined; the regulatory section says the ownership objection is weaker under EBA GL/2020/06 but the walkthrough, ROI and A to H split are US-only. The corrected analogue from the EBA clone (only one of 103 mortgage Q&As touches loan-origination scope; 2 to 3 per year since 2024) suggests the EU owner-level loop is even smaller than stated, but the bank-internal EU desk remains unexamined.

The buyer and the user are the same one to three people at a mid-size lender (the senior underwriters who answer the desk), so H8 applies at the seat level: the product would sell a sub-FTE labour saving to the person whose labour it saves. The deep dive names a buyer but does not confront the seat count.

Privacy and access cost of the proposed base-rate experiment (GLBA and Regulation P NPI in scenario emails [RECALL, unverified]) is not addressed, yet cheap access is the sole reason given for the ranking.

Fair-lending pressure on discretionary exceptions (ECOA and Regulation B [RECALL, unverified]) tends to convert repeated exceptions into bright-line policy or stop them, as the cluster verifier noted for bank credit policy; the same force shrinks lender-policy H over time rather than letting a ledger compound. The deep dive lists fair lending as a mild positive for an exception register but not as a negative for recurrence.
corrected_verdict: Evidence against, not merely weak evidence leaning negative, for the lender-side underwriting help-desk as a standalone Sophon market, and the workflow should not hold a top-three slot on the basis of cheap sampling, which is asserted rather than shown. Structural reasons survive checking: the operative guide is owned, executed and increasingly self-encoded by the GSEs and FHA (AUS names and result codes verified in the CFPB HMDA spec; owner worksheets, Ask Poli, Income Calculator and AIM by recall); the lender's own layer is bright-line policy already carried in the overlay matrix and PPE (recall; the LoanScope demonstration is one developer's model and the Encompass API artefacts show no rules-export path); the only owner-level loop that could be measured (EBA Q&A, recomputed) is tiny, slow and irrelevant to underwriting; and the whole desk at a 10,000-loan lender is about 0.6 FTE (estimate from the deep dive's own inputs), so no H share rescues the economics. Every volume, repeat-rate and cost figure remains recall or estimate; nothing here is measurement. If money is spent at all: one lender, 300 to 500 desk questions, coded by that lender's senior underwriter, counting as H only lender-policy questions the overlay matrix does not already answer; continue only if categories 7 and 8 together exceed 25 percent, a clear majority of those concern lender policy the matrix is silent on, and each settled class recurs at least ten times a year; expect to stop.
overall: The deep dive's sourced items check out on their face (EBA counts and 317-day median reproduced from a fresh clone; HMDA fields 68 to 72, 96 to 107 and the 'millions of records' line verified against CFPB repos; LoanScope quotes verbatim; the ROI arithmetic is correct on its stated inputs), but three of its uses of that evidence fail: the EBA corpus cannot bracket lender-desk recurrence because only one of its 103 mortgage Q&As touches origination and the flow is 2 to 3 per year and falling; the Encompass API artefacts (one npm test-org package, one Activepieces piece, one lender SDK manifest) show no business-rules surface and so do not support the ledger's export path; and mortctl is a calculator, not a rule encoder. The FHA Refer penalty is real but undistinguishing because a human signs every agency file; the HMDA denial anchor says nothing about desk composition; the H range is an upper bound on a thinner increment over the existing overlay matrix; and the sole reason for the third-place ranking, cheap access to a log, is unproven and faces NPI constraints. The strongest negative the deep dive underplays is its own arithmetic: the whole desk is sub-FTE at a mid-size lender. Corrected verdict: evidence against a standalone product for this workflow; H3, H4, H6 and H8 supported structurally, H1 and H2 unmeasured, all figures recall or estimate under a prominent evidence limitation (WebSearch exhausted, all primary hosts blocked, sourced checks limited to GitHub and npm artefacts).
